lede: (five craft words the customer meets on every listing and nobody defines. The word is the hero; the piece is the example.)
idea: Across 498 competitor creatives no brand uses setting, cut or finishing as a theme. So teach the words. Each card is a dictionary entry — headword, respelled pronunciation, part of speech, one numbered sense, an etymology — over a macro plate of the piece that demonstrates the word. The format is one the reader already owns, and it puts Naira on the craft side of the table before it sells anything.
type: Velista caps headword at 168/186px with the respelling in mono and n./adj. in Cormorant italic, exactly as a dictionary abbreviates. Sense in Jost 30/35px with a numbered 1. Etymology in italic. Running head above the entry, guide words (pavé · pear) in the top strip where a dictionary page carries them. The product and price move into the foot in the same grammar as the earlier volumes.
review: Pass 1: the bottom third was empty and the guide words sat over the photograph. Fixed by putting the top strip on paper, the plate under it, and promoting the see-line into a product/price foot. Pass 2: the story headline clipped on BAGUETTE and BAROQUE and three cards ended on an orphaned word — abbreviated the part of speech and set text-wrap: pretty.
verdict: the etymology on BAROQUE is the best line in the set; the toggle plate was generated fresh because the archive never showed the bar through the ring.

E1.title: pavé
E1.why: “Stones set so close together that the metal beneath them disappears.” The plate is the extreme macro of the Prism Rivière from the July detail run, two stones sharp and the rest falling away, each in its own pavé halo.
E1.check: three colours only in the sharp stones; halos intact

E2.title: baguette
E2.why: A long rectangular step cut set edge to edge in a channel. The plate is the website's own macro of the Baguette Arc Hoops, the channel running the whole way round with no claws.

E3.title: huggie
E3.why: A small hinged hoop that snaps flush against the lobe. The plate shows the hinge seam on the front huggie, which is the whole point of the word.
E3.check: brushed satin, no stones, hinge visible

E4.title: toggle
E4.why: A clasp that closes with a turn: a straight bar passed through a ring and pulled flat. The archive held 147 frames of this chain and not one showed the bar through the ring, so this plate was generated fresh on ivory plaster with two lights and a 15mm scale cue.
E4.check: plain bar, plain ring, 4mm paperclip links, no stones

E5.title: baroque
E5.why: Of a pearl: irregular, not round, no two alike. The word came from the pearl before it came to art — Portuguese barroco, a misshapen pearl — which is the kind of fact only a jeweller gets to say.
E5.check: flat baroque shell pearls with gold spacer beads; no water claim on this non-waterproof piece
